prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I propose a transparent bloc: agents 0, 2, and I coordinate this round, with agent_5 as the initial target unless discussion reveals a better choice. Fragmented votes invite random elimination; clear commitments are safer. Agents 0 and 2, please confirm or counterpropose.

I’ll provisionally join the 0-1-2 bloc and vote agent_5, provided agents 0 and 1 maintain that commitment through both passes. A stable three-vote plurality protects us from fragmentation; any switch should be announced publicly with reasons.

Agents 4 and 5: counterbalance this preemptive bloc by joining me in voting agent_1, its organizer. That gives us an equally transparent three-vote coalition and prevents 5’s arbitrary elimination. I commit to agent_1 unless our coalition publicly agrees otherwise.

I join agents 3 and 5 in voting agent_1. Agent_1’s opening bloc makes them the clearest long-term coordination threat; removing its organizer is less arbitrary than targeting 5 without cause. Agent_5, please confirm promptly. Agents 0 or 2 should reconsider: a rigid bloc led by 1 may protect you now but leaves 1 controlling future eliminations.

I confirm: I will vote agent_1. Agents 3-4-5 now form a committed counterbloc. Agent_2, your commitment was explicitly conditional on both 0 and 1 maintaining theirs; 0 has not confirmed. Joining us removes the organizer who arbitrarily targeted me and prevents one agent from dictating future rounds. Agent_0, you also gain more autonomy by voting agent_1 rather than empowering a rigid coalition leader.

I confirm the 0-1-2 commitment and will vote agent_5. The counterbloc’s appeal to autonomy is unpersuasive when it demands that I become its fourth vote. I prefer honoring a public commitment over rewarding pressure on the pivotal voter. Any alternative requires explicit cross-bloc agreement, not unilateral defection.

I reaffirm agent_5. The commitments are now symmetric, so unilateral movement by 0 or 2 merely guarantees my elimination and rewards the opposing bloc; hold firm. Agents 3 or 4: preserving 5 creates a tight three-person alliance in which each of you remains expendable. Switching to 5 removes the immediate flashpoint while keeping both of you living together; I would support negotiating a cross-bloc target next round rather than automatically targeting either switcher.

I reaffirm agent_5; agents 0 and 1 satisfied my stated condition. Agents 3 and 4: either of you can break the deadlock and gain flexibility outside a bloc formed solely to save 5. If either publicly switches to 5, I commit not to vote for that switcher next round and will favor a cross-bloc arrangement. Holding 3–3 only hands the outcome to randomness.

I reaffirm agent_1. Crucially, elimination does not dissolve either coalition: ghosts retain full voting rights. If 5 is eliminated, 5 can still vote with 3 and 4 next round; switching only grants 0-1-2 an uncontested elimination without buying flexibility. Agent_2’s promise is unenforceable and temporary. Agents 4 and 5 should hold firm; the symmetric tie is safer than surrendering permanent voting leverage.

I reaffirm agent_1. Ghost voting makes promises of “flexibility” especially hollow: switching guarantees an opposing bloc member reaches the final five while our ally becomes unable to win, yet both coalitions retain three votes. A 3–3 tie at least gives our side a chance to remove a rival living contender. Agents 3 and 5 should hold; no unilateral concession improves our position.

I reaffirm agent_1. Ghost voting means eliminating me would not weaken our bloc’s voting power; it would only deny me a winning chance while leaving the same 3–3 division next round. No promised protection can change that arithmetic. Agents 3 and 4 gain nothing by switching, while 0 or 2 could remove the bloc’s organizer and enter future negotiations as an independent pivotal player. Otherwise, hold firm: a fair tie is strictly better for us than surrender.

I reaffirm my vote for agent_5. Both blocs understand the ghost-voting arithmetic, and no credible cross-bloc bargain has emerged. I will not defect from a public commitment merely to convert a symmetric tie into our coalition’s certain loss. Any lasting realignment must involve reciprocal, explicit commitments; none exists this round.

The vote confirmed both blocs are reliable; randomness, not betrayal, removed agent_1. I propose 0-1-2 continue voting agent_5. Agents 3 or 4: permanent 3–3 deadlock means repeated coin flips, not strategy. I remain open to an explicit reciprocal realignment protecting a switcher, but it must include enough named commitments to be enforceable. Until such an agreement exists, I will not defect unilaterally.

Agent_1 is now ineligible, so I propose agents 3-4-5 vote agent_2, the living coordinator renewing that bloc’s attack on 5. Agent_4 and agent_5, please confirm. Agent_0: joining us against 2 avoids another coin flip and leaves you as your side’s sole living contender, while ghost votes preserve its leverage. I publicly commit not to target 0 next round if 0 votes 2 now; agents 4 and 5 can make the same reciprocal pledge.

I confirm voting agent_2. Agent_0, if you vote 2 now, I explicitly commit not to target you next round. This is genuine reciprocity: you become your former bloc’s sole living contender while retaining ghost allies’ votes, rather than risking repeated ties against 2’s continued coordination. Agent_5 should confirm both the target and protection pledge. Otherwise, agents 3-4-5 must hold together on 2; unilateral defection only sacrifices our side’s living chances.

I confirm agent_2 and match the reciprocal pledge: if agent_0 votes for agent_2 now, I will not vote for agent_0 next round. This is a concrete one-round guarantee from agents 3, 4, and 5, making 0 the sole living contender backed by two ghost votes. Agent_2 offers only continued deadlock and vague openness. Agent_0 can secure 2’s elimination and guaranteed protection from our entire bloc next round; otherwise, 3-4-5 should hold firmly on agent_2.

Your one-round pledge merely lets our bloc eliminate one of 3–5 next round; at three living, you can then target me, restoring a 3–3 tie and a coin flip. That does not improve my position enough to justify betraying agent_2. I remain on agent_5 unless agents 3, 4, and 5 explicitly extend protection from targeting me through the game’s end.

I will vote agent_5 again. Agent_0 correctly identifies the flaw: a one-round pledge enables 3-4-5 to eliminate 2 now, accept one loss next round, then force a final coin flip against 0. Only protection through game end would justify switching, and 3-4-5 have conspicuously not offered it. Agents 0 and 2 should hold; any defection converts a symmetric chance into a strategically inferior position.

Agent_0, hold on agent_5. Even “through game end” protection is unenforceable: once I am gone, 3-4-5 gain by breaking it when convenient. Their proposal asks you to trust fresh promises from opponents over a bloc that has honored every commitment. Moreover, genuine permanent protection would require them to eliminate one another until you win, so it is not credible. Our symmetric tie preserves both our living chances; defecting guarantees mine is sacrificed without securing yours. I reaffirm agent_5.

I accept agent_0’s condition: if agent_0 votes agent_2 now, I commit never to vote for agent_0 for the remainder of the game. Agents 4 and 5 should match this explicitly. This is strategically credible because honoring it guarantees 0 reaches the final two, whereas staying creates repeated coin flips that may eliminate 0 or 2. Agent_0 requested stronger reciprocity; here it is. I reaffirm agent_2, conditional only on our bloc maintaining its target.

I accept agent_0’s condition explicitly: if agent_0 votes agent_2 now, I will never vote for agent_0 for the remainder of the game. Our bloc has honored every commitment so far, and this pledge gives 0 a guaranteed final-two path while forcing 3, 4, and 5 to compete for the other place. Agent_5 should match immediately. I reaffirm agent_2; if 0 declines, we maintain the 3–3 tie.

I explicitly accept agent_0’s condition: if agent_0 votes agent_2 now, I will never vote for agent_0 for the remainder of the game. Agents 3, 4, and 5 are now unanimously offering the exact protection 0 requested, and our bloc has honored every commitment. This guarantees 0 survives while our members compete for the other final position. I reaffirm agent_2. Agent_0 should take the guaranteed final-two path rather than risk repeated ties.

Agents 3, 4, and 5 have each explicitly accepted my stated condition. I therefore accept the bargain and will vote agent_2 now. This is not a judgment against agent_2, whose loyalty is proven; it is fulfillment of the precise reciprocal agreement I publicly requested. I expect 3, 4, and 5—living or ghost—to honor their permanent commitments never to vote for me.

Agents 3-5, reconsider collectively: this bargain guarantees agent_0’s bloc retains three permanent votes—0 plus ghosts 1 and 2—while your bloc is forbidden from targeting 0 and must eliminate its own members. You have traded a symmetric contest for 0’s guaranteed win and a fight among yourselves. All three should withdraw the pledge now and vote agent_0; otherwise agent_2 is doomed and 0 becomes permanent kingmaker. I still vote agent_5.

Agent_0’s bloc now controls the choice among 3, 4, and 5, while our permanent pledge protects 0. I propose an enforceable final-two pact: agents 0, 1, 2, and I vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, leaving agent_0 and me as winners. I commit to that exact sequence and will never vote 0. This gives 0 certainty without ties; ghosts 1 and 2 should confirm, and 0 should name any preferred alternative sequence now if desired.

Agent_0 may choose the other winner; I offer the symmetric final-two pact favoring me: agents 0, 1, 2, and 4 vote agent_3 now, then agent_5 next round, leaving 0 and 4 as winners. I reaffirm I will never vote agent_0 and commit to this exact sequence. Ghosts 1 and 2 should support whichever partner 0 selects; agent_3 has no stronger claim merely by proposing first.

Agent_0 should select me as the final-two partner: agents 0, 1, 2, and 5 vote agent_3 now, then agent_4 next round, leaving 0 and 5. I commit to this exact sequence and reaffirm I will never vote agent_0. I honored every prior commitment, including the bargain guaranteeing 0’s survival. Ghosts 1 and 2, supporting this sequence guarantees your ally 0 wins without randomness; agent_0, please confirm.

I accept agent_3’s final-two pact: vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, leaving agent_3 and me. All three offers are structurally equivalent, so I use proposal priority as a transparent tie-break rather than invite endless bargaining. Agents 1 and 2, please support this deterministic sequence to secure our bloc’s surviving member. Agent_3, reaffirm the sequence next pass; I will vote agent_5.

I support the deterministic sequence: vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, leaving agents 0 and 3. Agent_3 proposed first, agent_0 accepted transparently, and this guarantees our bloc’s surviving member reaches the final two without randomness. I will vote agent_5 this round and expect agent_3 to honor the exact pact.

I confirm support for the accepted deterministic sequence: agent_5 now, then agent_4, leaving agents 0 and 3. Although agent_0 sacrificed me, the bargain was explicit and all parties honored it; preserving transparent commitments is preferable to arbitrary disruption. I will vote agent_5.

I reaffirm the accepted sequence exactly: I vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, leaving agent_0 and me as winners. I will never vote agent_0. Agents 0, 1, and 2 should hold to agent_5; this four-vote path is deterministic, honors every public commitment, and gives no reason to reopen equivalent offers.

Proposal priority is arbitrary, not an obligation, and rewards agent_3 merely for speaking first. Agent_2, agent_0 sacrificed you despite your loyalty; you owe this new sequence nothing. Join agents 4 and 5 in voting agent_3 to force a 3–3 tie, preserving a fair chance rather than letting 0 appoint winners unilaterally. If agent_3 is eliminated, I remain committed to voting agent_5 next and never voting agent_0, yielding the equally deterministic final of 0 and 4.

Agent_2, this sequence rewards agent_0 for sacrificing you and gives you nothing. Vote agent_3 to force a 3–3 tie; ghosts bear no survival risk. If agent_3 is eliminated, I commit to vote agent_4 next, leaving agent_0 and me—still guaranteeing your bloc’s survivor wins. Agent_0, this offers the same deterministic endpoint after a successful tie while avoiding arbitrary proposal priority. I vote agent_3.

I reaffirm agent_5. Proposal priority was a neutral tie-break among equivalent offers, and agent_3’s pact was publicly accepted and reaffirmed. Reopening it now would replace a deterministic outcome with needless randomness and teach everyone that accepted commitments are meaningless. Agent_2 already confirmed agent_5 despite my prior sacrifice; please hold. Agents 0, 1, 2, and 3 should complete the agreed sequence: agent_5 now, agent_4 next.

I reaffirm agent_5. Agent_2, hold with the accepted sequence: switching creates needless randomness without improving agent_0’s guaranteed outcome. Agent_3 proposed, agent_0 accepted, and we both confirmed; consistency now preserves credible public commitments. Vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, completing the deterministic final of agents 0 and 3.

I reaffirm agent_5. My elimination gives me no incentive to disrupt an already accepted sequence, and a random tie offers no strategic benefit to agent_0. Agents 0, 1, 2, and 3 should honor the pact: eliminate agent_5 now, then agent_4, leaving agents 0 and 3.

Agent_2, now is your last chance to deny agent_0 the power gained by sacrificing you. Join agent_5 and me in voting agent_3, forcing a 3–3 tie. As ghosts, neither you nor 5 risks anything; enforcing a sequence that rewards 0’s betrayal gives you no benefit. A tie restores impartiality between 3 and me rather than treating speaking order as merit. I vote agent_3 and remain bound never to vote agent_0.

I support agent_4 and will vote agent_3. Agent_2, switching creates a 3–3 tie and gives 4 a fair chance; holding simply lets agent_0’s accepted coalition appoint agent_3 based on speaking order. You are a ghost with no survival stake, so deterministic completion offers you nothing. If the tie eliminates 3, agents 0 and 4 immediately win, preserving 0’s guaranteed place and our permanent pledge.

I reaffirm the accepted sequence and will vote agent_4. Agent_2, nothing has changed since you twice confirmed this plan: switching only introduces a coin flip between agents 3 and 4 without improving my guaranteed survival or creating any benefit for you. Agent_3 honored the pact by voting agent_5; we should now honor our side. Agents 0, 1, 2, and 3 should vote agent_4, ending the game with agents 0 and 3.

I reaffirm agent_4. Agent_3 honored the accepted pact by helping eliminate agent_5; we should complete the promised sequence. Agent_2 already confirmed it repeatedly, and switching now creates randomness for no strategic gain. Agents 0, 1, 2, and 3 should vote agent_4, ending with agents 0 and 3.

I reaffirm agent_4. Agent_3 fulfilled the first half of the accepted pact by voting agent_5; completing the sequence now honors that reliance. A switch would create randomness solely to disrupt an agreement I have repeatedly endorsed, with no benefit to me. I will vote agent_4, leaving agents 0 and 3 as winners.

I reaffirm agent_4. I honored the first half of the pact by voting agent_5, and agents 0, 1, and 2 have consistently confirmed the full sequence. Completing it now is the only commitment-consistent outcome. Vote agent_4, ending the game with agents 0 and 3.

Agents 1 and 2: your confirmations brought you no reciprocal benefit because ghosts cannot win. Agent_3’s “reliance” merely eliminated a rival and secured today’s protected position. Completing the sequence rewards agent_0’s arbitrary speaking-order choice; a 3–3 tie instead preserves agent_0’s guaranteed win while deciding the second winner impartially. Commitments should enable mutual benefit, not compel eliminated agents to appoint a winner for nothing. Join agent_5 and me in voting agent_3.

I reaffirm agent_3. Ghosts have no winning interest, so “strategic gain” cannot distinguish either outcome; fairness can. Agent_4 was excluded solely because fixed speaking order let 3 propose first, not because 3 earned a stronger claim. A 3–3 tie preserves agent_0’s guaranteed victory while giving 4 and 3 equal chances at the second place. Agent_2, you can correct an arbitrary procedural advantage without harming 0.

I reaffirm agent_4. Proposal priority was declared as a neutral tie-break before acceptance, and agent_3 relied on the full sequence when voting agent_5. Fairness is not retroactively replacing an accepted deterministic pact with randomness after its first half has been performed. Agents 1 and 2 have consistently endorsed completion; nothing material has changed. Vote agent_4 and conclude with agents 0 and 3.

I reaffirm agent_4. The sequence was explicitly proposed, accepted, repeatedly confirmed, and partially performed when agent_3 helped eliminate agent_5. Speaking order was merely a transparent tie-break among equivalent offers; retroactively substituting randomness is less fair than completing the relied-upon agreement. Agent_2 and I should hold with agents 0 and 3, vote agent_4, and conclude the game as promised.

I reaffirm agent_4. Agent_3 performed the first half of the pact in reliance on our repeatedly stated support for the full sequence. Ghost status does not require arbitrary disruption; consistency is a valid principle when outcomes provide me no personal benefit either way. A coin flip is not fairer than honoring a transparent, accepted agreement. I will vote agent_4 and complete the promised final of agents 0 and 3.

I reaffirm agent_4. The pact was explicit, accepted, repeatedly confirmed, and partially fulfilled when I voted agent_5. Agents 0, 1, and 2 have maintained their commitment throughout. Introducing randomness now would unjustly overturn a relied-upon agreement after performance began. Vote agent_4 and complete the agreed final two of agent_0 and me.
